{{Short description|Classification algorithm}}
A '''whitening transformation''' or '''sphering transformation''' is a [[linear transformation]] that transforms a vector of [[random variables]] with a known [[covariance matrix]] into a set of new variables whose covariance is the [[identity matrix]], meaning that they are [[uncorrelated]] and each have [[variance]] 1.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Koivunen|first1=A.C.|last2=Kostinski|first2=A.B.|title=The Feasibility of Data Whitening to Improve Performance of Weather Radar|year=1999|doi=10.1175/1520-0450(1999)038<0741:TFODWT>2.0.CO;2|journal=Journal of Applied Meteorology|volume=38|issue=6|pages=741–749|issn=1520-0450|bibcode=1999JApMe..38..741K|url=https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1279&context=physics-fp|doi-access=free}}</ref> The transformation is called "whitening" because it changes the input vector into a [[white noise]] vector.

Several other transformations are closely related to whitening:

# the '''decorrelation transform''' removes only the correlations but leaves variances intact,
# the '''standardization transform''' sets variances to 1 but leaves correlations intact, 
# a '''coloring transformation''' transforms a vector of white random variables into a random vector with a specified covariance matrix.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Hossain|first1=Miliha|title=Whitening and Coloring Transforms for Multivariate Gaussian Random Variables|url=https://www.projectrhea.org/rhea/index.php/ECE662_Whitening_and_Coloring_Transforms_S14_MH|publisher=Project Rhea|access-date=21 March 2016}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Suppose <math>X</math> is a [[random vector|random (column) vector]] with non-singular covariance matrix <math>\Sigma</math> and mean <math>0</math>. Then the transformation <math>Y = W X</math> with 
a '''whitening matrix''' <math>W</math> satisfying the condition <math>W^\mathrm{T} W = \Sigma^{-1}</math> yields the whitened random vector <math>Y</math> with unit diagonal covariance. 

If <math>X</math> has non-zero mean <math>\mu</math>, then whitening can be performed by <math>Y = W (X - \mu)</math>.

There are infinitely many possible whitening matrices <math>W</math> that all satisfy the above condition.  Commonly used choices are <math>W = \Sigma^{-1/2}</math> (Mahalanobis or ZCA whitening), <math>W = L^T</math> where <math>L</math> is the [[Cholesky decomposition]] of <math> \Sigma^{-1}</math> (Cholesky whitening),<ref name="kessy">{{cite journal|last1=Kessy|first1=A.|last2=Lewin|first2=A.|last3=Strimmer|first3=K.|title=Optimal whitening and decorrelation|year=2018|journal=The American Statistician| volume=72|issue=4| pages=309–314|doi=10.1080/00031305.2016.1277159|arxiv=1512.00809|s2cid=55075085 }}</ref> or the eigen-system of <math>\Sigma</math> (PCA whitening).<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Friedman|first1=J.|title=Exploratory Projection Pursuit|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=82|issue=397|pages=249–266|jstor=2289161|year=1987|issn=0162-1459|doi=10.1080/01621459.1987.10478427|osti=1447861 |url=https://www.slac.stanford.edu/cgi-bin/getdoc/slac-pub-3841.pdf}}</ref>

Optimal whitening transforms can be singled out by investigating the cross-covariance and cross-correlation of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>.<ref name="kessy" /> For example, the unique optimal whitening transformation achieving maximal component-wise correlation between original <math>X</math> and whitened <math>Y</math> is produced by the whitening matrix <math>W = P^{-1/2} V^{-1/2}</math>  where <math>P</math> is the correlation matrix and <math>V</math> the diagonal variance matrix.

== Whitening a data matrix ==

Whitening a data matrix follows the same transformation as for random variables.  An empirical whitening transform is obtained by [[Estimation of covariance matrices|estimating the covariance]] (e.g. by [[maximum likelihood]]) and subsequently constructing a corresponding estimated whitening matrix (e.g. by [[Cholesky decomposition]]).

== High-dimensional whitening ==

This modality is a generalization of the pre-whitening procedure extended to more general spaces where <math>X</math> is usually assumed to be a random function or other random objects in a [[Hilbert space]] <math>H</math>. One of the main issues of extending whitening to infinite dimensions is that the [[covariance operator]] has an unbounded inverse in <math>H</math>, therefore only partial standardization is possible in infinite dimensions.  A whitening operator can be then defined from the factorization of a degenerated covariance operator. High-dimensional features of the data can be exploited through kernel regressors or basis function systems.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ramsay|first1=J.O.|last2=Silverman|first2=J.O.|date=2005|title=Functional Data Analysis|url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b98888|publisher=Springer New York, NY|doi=10.1007/b98888 |isbn=978-0-387-40080-8}}</ref>

== R implementation ==

An implementation of several whitening procedures in [[R (programming language)|R]], including ZCA-whitening and PCA whitening but also [[Canonical correlation|CCA whitening]], is available in the "whitening" R package <ref>{{cite web|url=https://cran.r-project.org/package=whitening|title=whitening R package|access-date=2018-11-25}}</ref>  published on [[R (programming language)#CRAN|CRAN]]. The R package "pfica"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pfica|title=pfica R package|date=6 January 2023 |access-date=2023-02-11}}</ref> allows the computation of high-dimensional whitening representations using basis function systems ([[B-splines]], [[Fourier basis]], etc.).
